decks.title: Digestion and Absorption — Part 1: The alimentary canal and digestive glands
goals: Trace the human alimentary canal from mouth to anus
Describe human teeth and work with the dental formula
Describe the four layers of the gut wall, villi and microvilli
Describe the salivary glands, liver and pancreas and their ducts

slides.heading: Digestion and Absorption
slides.body_md: Part 1 — the organs of the digestive system. This chapter is CBSE reading material for formative (school) assessment only.

visual.alt: Flow from ingestion through digestion, absorption and assimilation to egestion

slides.narration: Our food contains carbohydrates, proteins and fats, which are too large to be used directly. Digestion breaks them into simple, absorbable substances, by mechanical and biochemical methods. The digestive system has two parts: the alimentary canal and the associated glands.

slides.heading: What digestion must achieve
slides.body_md: Biomacromolecules in food must be converted into small, soluble units before they can be absorbed.

rows: Monosaccharides such as glucose, fructose, galactose

visual.alt: Table of food components and their absorbable end products

slides.narration: Each large molecule has its own end products. Starch ends as glucose, proteins as amino acids, fats as fatty acids and glycerol, and nucleic acids as sugars and bases. Enzymes from several glands do this work along the canal.

slides.heading: The human alimentary canal
slides.body_md: The canal runs from the **mouth** to the **anus**: buccal cavity, pharynx, oesophagus, stomach, small intestine and large intestine. The **salivary glands, liver and pancreas** pour secretions into it.

slides.narration: Follow the canal from the mouth. Food passes through the pharynx and the long oesophagus into the J shaped stomach, then the C shaped duodenum, the coiled jejunum and ileum, and finally the caecum, colon and rectum. The liver, gall bladder and pancreas lie close to the duodenum.

slides.heading: The mouth: teeth and tongue
slides.body_md: The mouth leads into the **buccal (oral) cavity**, which has teeth and a muscular **tongue**.

rows: Each tooth is embedded in a socket of the jaw bone
Two sets of teeth: milk (deciduous) teeth replaced by permanent teeth
Teeth of four types: incisors, canines, premolars, molars
Hard chewing surface that helps in mastication
Freely movable muscular organ attached to the floor by the frenulum; papillae, some with taste buds

visual.alt: Table of features of human teeth and tongue

slides.narration: Human teeth are set in sockets, come in two sets during life, and are of four kinds. The hard enamel surface grinds food. The tongue is attached to the floor of the mouth by a fold called the frenulum, and some of its small projections, the papillae, carry taste buds.

slides.heading: The dental formula
slides.body_md: The arrangement of teeth in each half of the upper and lower jaw, in the order I, C, PM, M, is the **dental formula**: **2123/2123** for an adult human.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: reading the dental formula
slides.body_md: Use the formula 2123/2123 to find (i) the total number of teeth and (ii) the percentage of them that are molars.
bullets: (i) One half jaw: $2 + 1 + 2 + 3 = 8$; four half jaws: $8 \times 4 = 32$.
(ii) Molars: $3 \times 4 = 12$; $\dfrac{12}{32} \times 100 = 37.5$ percent.
The formula always describes **one half** of each jaw, so multiply by four.

visual.alt: Worked table: 32 teeth, 12 molars

slides.narration: Two plus one plus two plus three is eight teeth in each half jaw. There are four half jaws, so thirty-two teeth in all. Three molars in each half give twelve molars, which is thirty-seven and a half percent of the set.

slides.heading: Pharynx, oesophagus and stomach
slides.body_md: The pharynx is a **common passage for food and air**; the **epiglottis** stops food entering the glottis during swallowing.

rows: Thin, long tube through the neck, thorax and diaphragm; opens into the stomach through the gastro-oesophageal sphincter
J-shaped bag in the upper left abdomen: cardiac portion (oesophagus opens here), fundic region, pyloric portion
Guards the opening of the stomach into the duodenum

visual.alt: Table of the oesophagus, stomach regions and pyloric sphincter

slides.narration: Both the oesophagus and the windpipe open into the pharynx, so swallowing must be coordinated. The cartilage flap called the epiglottis covers the glottis while food passes. The stomach then receives food at its cardiac end and releases it at the pyloric end.

slides.heading: Small and large intestines
slides.body_md: The **small intestine** has three regions; the **large intestine** has three parts.

rows: Highly coiled; opens into the large intestine
Small blind sac with symbiotic micro-organisms; the vestigial vermiform appendix arises from it
Ascending, transverse, descending and sigmoid parts

visual.alt: Table of the regions of the small and large intestines

slides.narration: Remember the small intestine in order: duodenum, jejunum, ileum. The large intestine begins with the caecum, which carries the narrow vermiform appendix, continues as the four parts of the colon, and ends in the rectum.

slides.heading: The wall of the alimentary canal
slides.body_md: From the oesophagus to the rectum the wall has four layers: **serosa, muscularis, sub-mucosa and mucosa**.

slides.narration: Outside is the serosa, a thin mesothelium. Next come the muscle layers, usually inner circular and outer longitudinal. The sub-mucosa carries nerves, blood and lymph vessels. The mucosa lines the lumen, forming irregular folds called rugae in the stomach and finger-like villi in the small intestine.

slides.heading: Villi and microvilli
slides.body_md: Cells lining the villi bear **microvilli**, giving a **brush border**. Each villus has a network of **capillaries** and a large lymph vessel, the **lacteal**. Goblet cells secrete mucus; crypts lie between the villi.

slides.narration: A villus is a tiny finger of the mucosa. Its surface cells are covered in microvilli, which make the surface look like a brush. Inside, blood capillaries collect sugars and amino acids, while the central lacteal collects fats. Together, villi and microvilli increase the surface area enormously.

slides.heading: Digestive glands
slides.body_md: Three kinds of glands pour secretions into the canal.

rows: Parotids (cheek), sub-maxillary or sub-mandibular (lower jaw), sub-linguals (below the tongue)
Largest gland, about 1.2 to 1.5 kg; two lobes below the diaphragm; hepatic lobules with Glisson’s capsule
Bile, stored and concentrated in the gall bladder
Between the limbs of the C-shaped duodenum; exocrine and endocrine
Alkaline pancreatic juice; insulin and glucagon

visual.alt: Table of salivary glands, liver and pancreas with positions and secretions

slides.narration: Saliva comes from three pairs of salivary glands. The liver, the largest gland of the body, makes bile in its hepatic lobules. The pancreas is both exocrine, making pancreatic juice, and endocrine, making the hormones insulin and glucagon.

slides.heading: How bile and pancreatic juice reach the duodenum

slides.narration: Bile leaves the liver along the hepatic duct and is stored in the gall bladder. When needed it flows down the cystic duct and the common bile duct. This joins the duct from the pancreas, and the two secretions enter the duodenum together through one opening controlled by the sphincter of Oddi.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: size and surface
slides.body_md: (i) An adult weighing 60 kg has a liver of 1.5 kg. What percentage of body mass is the liver? (ii) In a model, folds multiply the intestinal surface by 3, villi by 10 and microvilli by 20. What is the total factor? (Illustrative values.)
bullets: (i) $\dfrac{1.5}{60} \times 100 = 2.5$ percent.
(ii) $3 \times 10 \times 20 = 600$ times.
Real estimates of the surface gain vary between sources; the point is that the factors **multiply**.

visual.alt: Worked table: liver 2.5 percent of body mass; surface 600 times larger

slides.narration: One and a half kilograms out of sixty is two and a half percent, a large share for one gland. For the surface, the three factors multiply: three times ten times twenty is six hundred. That is why the small intestine, though narrow, absorbs so well.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Canal: buccal cavity → pharynx → oesophagus → stomach (cardiac, fundic, pyloric) → duodenum, jejunum, ileum → caecum, colon, rectum → anus.
Teeth: thecodont, diphyodont, heterodont; 32 permanent teeth; formula 2123/2123.
Wall: serosa, muscularis, sub-mucosa, mucosa (rugae, villi, microvilli, goblet cells, crypts).
Glands: three pairs of salivary glands; liver (bile, gall bladder); pancreas (pancreatic juice, insulin, glucagon).
Bile and pancreatic ducts open together through the hepato-pancreatic duct and sphincter of Oddi.

visual.alt: Summary table of key structures in Part 1

slides.narration: To recap: the canal runs from mouth to anus through regions with distinct jobs. Human teeth are thecodont, diphyodont and heterodont. The gut wall has four layers, and villi with microvilli give a huge surface. The salivary glands, liver and pancreas supply the digestive juices.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Write the **dental formula** as upper over lower jaw for **one half** of each jaw.
Name the **four wall layers** in order from outside.
Draw and label the **duct system** up to the **sphincter of Oddi**.
This chapter is assessed in school (formative) tests, not in a board paper.

decks.title: Digestion and Absorption — Part 2: Digestion, absorption and disorders
goals: Explain digestion in the mouth, stomach and small intestine with enzymes and products
Explain the mechanisms of absorption, including fats
State where substances are absorbed, and describe assimilation and egestion
Describe common digestive and nutritional disorders

slides.heading: Digestion, absorption and disorders
slides.body_md: Part 2 — how food is broken down along the canal, how the products are absorbed, and what can go wrong.

nodes.label: Small intestine: all completed and absorbed

visual.alt: Flow of digestion along the canal from mouth to large intestine

slides.narration: Digestion is a relay. Starch digestion starts in the mouth, protein digestion in the stomach, and the small intestine finishes everything and absorbs the products. The large intestine mainly absorbs water and minerals. The activities of the gut are controlled by nerves and local hormones.

slides.heading: Digestion in the mouth
slides.body_md: Teeth and tongue **masticate** food and mix it with saliva; mucus helps form a **bolus**, which is swallowed (**deglutition**) and carried down the oesophagus by **peristalsis**.

rows: Hydrolyses about 30 percent of starch to maltose at optimum pH 6.8
Lubricates and sticks food particles into a bolus

visual.alt: Table of the components of saliva and their roles

slides.narration: Chemical digestion begins in the mouth. Salivary amylase splits starch into the sugar maltose, which is why bread chewed for a while tastes sweet. Lysozyme protects against bacteria. Successive waves of muscle contraction, called peristalsis, then push the bolus down to the stomach.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: starch and acidity
slides.body_md: (i) A meal has 50 g of starch, and about 30 percent is hydrolysed in the mouth. How much is left for the intestine? (ii) Saliva works at pH 6.8 and gastric juice at pH 1.8. How many times more hydrogen ions does gastric juice have?
bullets: (i) $50 \times \dfrac{30}{100} = 15$ g hydrolysed; $50 - 15 = 35$ g left.
(ii) $6.8 - 1.8 = 5$ pH units, so $10^{5}$, that is 1,00,000 times.
Amylase stops working once the bolus is mixed with acid in the stomach.

visual.alt: Worked table: 15 grams hydrolysed, 35 grams left; stomach a hundred thousand times more acidic

slides.narration: Thirty percent of fifty grams is fifteen grams, so thirty-five grams of starch still reach the intestine. A difference of five pH units means ten multiplied by itself five times, one lakh times more hydrogen ions. No wonder salivary amylase cannot keep working in the stomach.

slides.heading: Quick check: saliva
slides.body_md: Which component of saliva is antibacterial?
slides.narration: Quick check. It is not an enzyme for food.

slides.heading: Digestion in the stomach
slides.body_md: Food is stored for **4 to 5 hours**, churned with acidic gastric juice and called **chyme**.

rows: With bicarbonates, lubricates and protects the lining from acid
Converted by HCl to pepsin: proteins to proteoses and peptones
HCl gives pH 1.8 for pepsin; intrinsic factor needed to absorb vitamin B12

visual.alt: Table of gastric gland cells, their secretions and roles

slides.narration: Pepsinogen is harmless until hydrochloric acid turns it into pepsin, which begins protein digestion. Mucus and bicarbonates shield the stomach wall from the acid. In infants, rennin helps digest milk proteins, and small amounts of lipase are also secreted.

slides.heading: Digestion in the small intestine
slides.body_md: Three secretions act here: **bile**, **pancreatic juice** and **intestinal juice (succus entericus)**. The medium is kept alkaline, about **pH 7.8**.

rows: Bile pigments (bilirubin, biliverdin), bile salts, cholesterol, phospholipids; emulsifies fats into micelles; activates lipases
Trypsinogen (activated by enterokinase to trypsin, which activates the rest), chymotrypsinogen, procarboxypeptidases, amylases, lipases, nucleases
Brush border and goblet cell secretions: maltase and other disaccharidases, dipeptidases, lipases, nucleosidases
Dipeptides to amino acids; maltose, lactose, sucrose to monosaccharides; fats to fatty acids and glycerol; nucleotides to sugars and bases

visual.alt: Table of bile, pancreatic juice and succus entericus with their actions

slides.narration: Most breakdown happens in the duodenum. Pancreatic enzymes turn proteins into dipeptides, starch into disaccharides and fats into glycerides, and enzymes of the brush border finish the job. Mucus and bicarbonate from the pancreas protect the lining and keep the medium alkaline.

slides.heading: How nutrients are absorbed
slides.body_md: Absorption moves end products through the intestinal mucosa into **blood or lymph**.

rows: Small amounts of glucose, amino acids, chloride ions
Facilitated transport (with carrier ions such as sodium ions)
Active transport (against the gradient, uses energy)

visual.alt: Table of absorption mechanisms and the substances they move

slides.narration: Some substances simply diffuse in when they are more concentrated in the gut. Others need carriers, or energy to move against the gradient. Water follows by osmosis. Fats need a special route, which we look at next.

slides.heading: Absorption of fats
slides.body_md: Fatty acids and glycerol are **insoluble**, so they cannot enter the blood directly.

visual.alt: Flow of fat absorption from micelles to chylomicrons, lacteals and blood

slides.narration: First the fatty acids and glycerol are packed into tiny droplets called micelles, which move into the mucosa. There they are rebuilt into protein coated fat globules called chylomicrons. These pass into the lacteal of each villus, and the lymph vessels finally empty them into the blood.

slides.heading: Quick check: fat absorption
slides.body_md: Choose the correct sequence for absorbing digested fat.
slides.narration: Quick check. Which comes first, micelles or chylomicrons?

slides.heading: Where absorption happens; assimilation and egestion
slides.body_md: The **small intestine** is the principal organ of absorption.

rows: Certain drugs, through the mucosa of the mouth and under the tongue
Glucose, fructose, fatty acids, glycerol, amino acids
Water, some minerals and drugs; no significant digestion; mucus binds and lubricates waste

visual.alt: Table of absorption in different parts of the canal

slides.narration: Absorbed substances reach the tissues, which use them: this is assimilation. Undigested waste enters the caecum through the ileo-caecal valve, which stops back flow, and is stored in the rectum. Its removal through the anus, called defaecation, is voluntary and is carried out by a mass peristaltic movement.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: energy from a snack
slides.body_md: A snack has 60 g of carbohydrate, 15 g of protein and 10 g of fat. Find its energy using (i) physiological fuel values 4, 4, 9 kcal per g and (ii) gross calorific values 4.1, 5.65, 9.45 kcal per g.
bullets: (i) $60 \times 4 + 15 \times 4 + 10 \times 9 = 390$ kcal, about 1632 kJ.
Gram for gram, fat gives more than twice the energy: 60 g of carbohydrate equals only about 26.7 g of fat.

visual.alt: Worked table: 390 kilocalories physiological, 425.25 gross

slides.narration: Using the body values, two hundred and forty plus sixty plus ninety gives three hundred and ninety kilocalories. The calorimeter gives more, about four hundred and twenty-five, because the body does not digest, absorb and oxidise everything completely. One kilocalorie is about four point two kilojoules.

slides.heading: Quick check: absorption
slides.body_md: Judge the assertion and the reason about the small intestine.
slides.narration: Quick check. Where is digestion completed?

slides.heading: Disorders of the digestive system
slides.body_md: Inflammation of the intestinal tract, often from **bacterial or viral infection**, is the most common ailment; parasites such as tapeworm, roundworm, threadworm, hookworm and pinworm also cause infections.

rows: Liver affected; skin and eyes turn yellow from deposited bile pigments
Ejection of stomach contents through the mouth; reflex controlled by the vomit centre in the medulla; usually preceded by nausea
Abnormal frequency of bowel movement and more liquid faeces; reduces absorption of food
Faeces retained in the rectum as bowel movements occur irregularly
Food not properly digested, feeling of fullness; from inadequate enzymes, anxiety, food poisoning, over-eating, spicy food

visual.alt: Table of digestive disorders with descriptions

slides.narration: Most digestive disorders are short-lived but can be serious in small children. Diarrhoea and vomiting quickly drain water and salts, so rehydration matters. Jaundice signals that the liver is not handling bile pigments properly.

slides.heading: Protein–energy malnutrition
slides.body_md: Diets lacking proteins and total food calories cause **protein–energy malnutrition (PEM)** in infants and children.

rows: Protein deficiency, enough calories (e.g. early weaning to a starchy diet)
Simultaneous deficiency of proteins and calories (mother’s milk replaced early by poor food)
Muscle wasting, thin limbs, poor growth and brain development, oedema and swelling
Extreme emaciation, thin limbs, dry thin wrinkled skin, impaired growth and brain development

visual.alt: Table comparing kwashiorkor and marasmus

slides.narration: The two forms of malnutrition look different. A child with kwashiorkor gets enough energy but too little protein, so the body swells with fluid. An infant with marasmus lacks both protein and energy, so the body wastes away with no swelling.

slides.heading: Quick check: malnutrition
slides.body_md: Identify the condition of the very thin infant with dry, wrinkled skin.
slides.narration: Quick check. Is there swelling, and are calories short too?

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Mouth: salivary amylase (pH 6.8) digests about 30 percent of starch to maltose; lysozyme; bolus, deglutition, peristalsis.
Stomach: HCl (pH 1.8) activates pepsinogen to pepsin; rennin in infants; mucus protects; chyme after 4 to 5 hours.
Small intestine (pH 7.8): bile emulsifies; enterokinase activates trypsin; pancreatic and brush-border enzymes finish digestion.
Absorption: diffusion, facilitated and active transport, osmosis; fats as micelles → chylomicrons → lacteals.
Disorders: jaundice, vomiting, diarrhoea, constipation, indigestion; PEM as kwashiorkor and marasmus.

visual.alt: Summary table of enzymes and end products

slides.narration: To recap: starch digestion starts in the mouth, protein digestion in the stomach, and the small intestine completes everything and absorbs it, fats taking the lymph route. Know the common digestive disorders and the two forms of protein energy malnutrition.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: State the **pH** at which each juice works: saliva 6.8, stomach 1.8, intestine 7.8.
Say that **bile has no enzymes**; it emulsifies fats and activates lipases.
Explain **enterokinase → trypsin → other enzymes** as a chain.
Compare **kwashiorkor** and **marasmus** by cause and signs.
slides.narration: Exam tips. Learn the working pH of saliva, gastric juice and intestinal juice. Remember bile has no enzymes. Explain how enterokinase starts the chain of enzyme activation. And compare kwashiorkor with marasmus by cause and by signs.

notes.title: Digestion and Absorption — Notes

sections.heading: 1. The alimentary canal
sections.body_md:
*This chapter is CBSE reading material for formative (school-based) assessment only; it is not examined in a board paper.*

Food (carbohydrates, proteins, fats) must be broken into simple, absorbable substances by **digestion**, using mechanical and biochemical methods. The digestive system consists of the **alimentary canal** and the **associated glands**.

**Mouth and teeth.** The mouth leads to the **buccal (oral) cavity**. Each tooth is embedded in a socket of the jaw bone (**thecodont**). Humans form two sets of teeth — milk (deciduous) teeth replaced by permanent teeth (**diphyodont**). An adult has **32 permanent teeth** of four types (**heterodont**): incisors (I), canines (C), premolars (PM) and molars (M). Their arrangement in each half of the upper and lower jaw, in the order I, C, PM, M, is the **dental formula, 2123/2123** (8 per half jaw × 4 = 32). The hard chewing surface is **enamel**. The **tongue** is a freely movable muscular organ attached to the floor of the oral cavity by the **frenulum**; its upper surface has **papillae**, some bearing taste buds.

**Pharynx and oesophagus.** The short pharynx is a **common passage for food and air**; the oesophagus and trachea open into it. The cartilaginous **epiglottis** prevents food entering the glottis during swallowing. The thin, long **oesophagus** passes through the neck, thorax and diaphragm into the stomach; the **gastro-oesophageal sphincter** regulates its opening.

**Stomach.** A J-shaped bag in the upper left abdomen with a **cardiac** portion (where the oesophagus opens), a **fundic** region and a **pyloric** portion that opens into the small intestine, guarded by the **pyloric sphincter**.

**Small intestine.** C-shaped **duodenum**, long coiled **jejunum** and highly coiled **ileum**, which opens into the large intestine.

**Large intestine.** The **caecum**, a small blind sac with some symbiotic micro-organisms, from which the vestigial **vermiform appendix** arises; the **colon** — ascending, transverse, descending and sigmoid; and the **rectum**, opening out through the **anus**.

sections.heading: 2. The wall of the gut, villi and microvilli
sections.body_md:
From the oesophagus to the rectum the wall has **four layers**:
- **Serosa** — outermost, a thin **mesothelium** (epithelium of visceral organs) with some connective tissue.
- **Muscularis** — smooth muscle, usually an **inner circular** and an **outer longitudinal** layer; an oblique layer in some regions.
- **Sub-mucosa** — loose connective tissue with **nerves, blood and lymph vessels**; in the duodenum it also has glands (Brunner’s glands).
- **Mucosa** — lines the lumen; forms irregular folds (**rugae**) in the stomach and finger-like **villi** in the small intestine. Cells lining the villi have **microvilli**, giving a **brush border**; these modifications increase the surface area enormously. Each villus has a network of **capillaries** and a large lymph vessel, the **lacteal**. **Goblet cells** secrete mucus for lubrication. The mucosa forms **gastric glands** in the stomach and **crypts** (crypts of Lieberkuhn) between the bases of villi in the intestine.

All four layers show modifications in different parts of the canal. (A simple model in this chapter multiplies the surface by 3 for folds, 10 for villi and 20 for microvilli, giving 600 times; published estimates vary.)

sections.heading: 3. Digestive glands
sections.body_md:
**Salivary glands.** Saliva is mainly produced by three pairs: the **parotids** (cheek), the **sub-maxillary or sub-mandibular** glands (lower jaw) and the **sub-linguals** (below the tongue).

**Liver.** The **largest gland** of the body, about **1.2 to 1.5 kg** in an adult human, situated just below the diaphragm, with **two lobes**. **Hepatic lobules**, with hepatic cells arranged in cords, are its structural and functional units; each lobule is covered by a thin connective tissue sheath, **Glisson’s capsule**. Bile secreted by hepatic cells passes through the **hepatic ducts** and is stored and concentrated in the **gall bladder**. The **cystic duct** of the gall bladder and the hepatic duct form the **common bile duct**.

**Pancreas.** A compound (exocrine and endocrine) elongated organ between the limbs of the C-shaped duodenum. The **exocrine** part secretes alkaline **pancreatic juice** with enzymes; the **endocrine** part secretes the hormones **insulin and glucagon**.

The bile duct and the **pancreatic duct** open together into the duodenum as the **common hepato-pancreatic duct**, guarded by the **sphincter of Oddi**.

sections.heading: 4. Digestion of food
sections.body_md:
**Mouth.** Teeth and tongue, with saliva, **masticate** and mix food; mucus helps form a **bolus**, which is swallowed (**deglutition**) and moved down the oesophagus by **peristalsis**; the gastro-oesophageal sphincter controls its entry into the stomach. Saliva contains electrolytes (sodium, potassium, chloride and bicarbonate ions), **salivary amylase** and **lysozyme**. About **30 percent of starch** is hydrolysed in the mouth by salivary amylase (optimum **pH 6.8**) into the disaccharide **maltose**. Lysozyme is an antibacterial agent.

**Stomach.** Gastric glands have **mucus neck cells** (mucus), **peptic or chief cells** (pepsinogen) and **parietal or oxyntic cells** (HCl and **intrinsic factor**, needed for absorption of vitamin B12). Food is stored for **4 to 5 hours** and, churned with acidic gastric juice, becomes **chyme**. HCl converts **pepsinogen** into **pepsin**, which converts proteins into **proteoses and peptones**; HCl provides the optimal **pH 1.8**. Mucus and bicarbonates protect the mucosa from excoriation by the acid. **Rennin** in the gastric juice of infants helps digest milk proteins; small amounts of lipases are also secreted.

**Small intestine.** Muscular movements mix food with **bile, pancreatic juice and intestinal juice**.
- **Bile** has bile pigments (bilirubin, biliverdin), bile salts, cholesterol and phospholipids but **no enzymes**; it **emulsifies fats** into very small **micelles** and **activates lipases**.
- **Pancreatic juice** has inactive **trypsinogen, chymotrypsinogen, procarboxypeptidases**, and **amylases, lipases and nucleases**. **Enterokinase** from the intestinal mucosa activates trypsinogen to **trypsin**, which activates the other enzymes.
- **Succus entericus** (secretions of the brush border cells and goblet cells) contains disaccharidases (e.g. maltase), dipeptidases, lipases and nucleosidases. Mucus and bicarbonates from the pancreas give an alkaline medium (**pH 7.8**); Brunner’s glands of the sub-mucosa help.

Breakdown of biomacromolecules occurs mainly in the **duodenum**; the simple products are absorbed in the **jejunum and ileum**. No significant digestion occurs in the **large intestine**. Gut activities are under **neural and hormonal control**: the sight, smell or presence of food stimulates saliva, and local hormones from the gastric and intestinal mucosa control the secretion of digestive juices.

Food mixed with acidic gastric juice in the stomach.
An intestinal enzyme that activates trypsinogen to trypsin.
Intestinal juice: secretions of brush border and goblet cells.

sections.heading: 5. Absorption, assimilation and egestion
sections.body_md:
**Absorption** is the process by which end products of digestion pass through the intestinal mucosa into the **blood or lymph**, by passive, active or facilitated transport.
- **Simple diffusion:** small amounts of glucose, amino acids and chloride ions, down a concentration gradient.
- **Facilitated transport:** fructose and some amino acids, with the help of carrier ions such as sodium ions.
- **Osmosis:** water, along the osmotic gradient.
- **Active transport:** against the concentration gradient, using energy — amino acids, glucose, sodium ions.
- **Fats:** fatty acids and glycerol are insoluble, so they form **micelles**, move into the mucosa, are re-formed into protein-coated **chylomicrons**, and pass into the **lacteals**, which release them into the blood.

**Where:** mouth (certain drugs through the mucosa and under the tongue); stomach (water, simple sugars, alcohol); **small intestine** (principal organ: glucose, fructose, fatty acids, glycerol, amino acids); large intestine (water, some minerals and drugs).

**Assimilation** is the use of absorbed substances by the tissues. The large intestine also secretes **mucus**, which sticks waste particles together and lubricates them. Undigested material enters the caecum through the **ileo-caecal valve** (preventing back flow) and is stored in the rectum. Faeces there start a neural reflex causing an urge to remove them; **defaecation** (egestion) is a **voluntary** process carried out by a **mass peristaltic movement**.

key_terms.definition_md: Absorption with the help of carrier ions such as sodium ions.
Protein-coated fat globules formed in the intestinal mucosa and carried into lacteals.
Use of absorbed substances by the tissues.
Voluntary egestion of faeces through the anus by a mass peristaltic movement.

sections.heading: 6. Nutritional and digestive disorders
sections.body_md:
**Calorific value of food.** Energy in food is measured in kilocalories (1 kcal = 4.184 kJ). Gross calorific values measured in a bomb calorimeter are about **4.1** (carbohydrate), **5.65** (protein) and **9.45** (fat) kcal per g; the energy the body actually obtains, the **physiological fuel values**, are about **4, 4 and 9** kcal per g. (Values are rounded and vary slightly between sources.)

**Protein–energy malnutrition (PEM)** affects infants and children whose diets lack proteins and total calories:
- **Kwashiorkor** — protein deficiency with adequate calories, often when mother’s milk is replaced too early by a high-calorie, low-protein diet: wasting of muscles, thinning of limbs, failure of growth and brain development, extensive **oedema** and swelling.
- **Marasmus** — simultaneous deficiency of **proteins and calories**, usually in infants under a year when mother’s milk is replaced too early by food poor in both: impaired growth, extreme **emaciation**, thin limbs, dry, thin and wrinkled skin; growth and brain development impaired.

**Digestive disorders.** Inflammation of the intestinal tract from **bacterial or viral infections** is the most common ailment; intestinal parasites (tapeworm, roundworm, threadworm, hookworm, pinworm) also cause infection.
- **Jaundice:** the liver is affected; skin and eyes turn yellow from deposited **bile pigments**.
- **Vomiting:** ejection of stomach contents through the mouth; a **reflex** controlled by the **vomit centre in the medulla**; nausea usually precedes it.
- **Diarrhoea:** abnormal frequency of bowel movement and increased liquidity of faeces; **reduces absorption** of food.
- **Constipation:** faeces retained in the rectum as bowel movements occur irregularly.
- **Indigestion:** food not properly digested, a feeling of fullness; caused by inadequate enzyme secretion, anxiety, food poisoning, over-eating and spicy food.

key_terms.definition_md: Protein deficiency with adequate calories in children; oedema and wasting.
Combined protein and calorie deficiency in infants; extreme emaciation.
Yellowing of skin and eyes from deposited bile pigments when the liver is affected.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Note:** this chapter is CBSE reading material for formative (school-based) assessment only; the items here follow the CBSE school-test pattern.

**Common mistakes**
- Writing the dental formula for the whole jaw (it is for one half of each jaw: 2123/2123, 32 teeth).
- Saying bile contains enzymes (it has none; it emulsifies fats and activates lipases).
- Saying pepsinogen is activated by enterokinase (HCl activates pepsinogen; enterokinase activates trypsinogen).
- Saying fats are absorbed directly into blood capillaries (they go as chylomicrons into lacteals).
- Placing most digestion in the large intestine (no significant digestion occurs there).
- Mixing up kwashiorkor (protein lack, oedema) and marasmus (protein and calorie lack, emaciation).

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1-mark items: name a gland, enzyme, product, region, layer, duct or disorder.
- 2–3-mark answers: dental features; gastric gland cells; activation of trypsin; role of bile; absorption mechanisms; fat absorption; two disorders compared.
- 5-mark answers: the alimentary canal and its wall; the digestive glands; digestion of food; absorption, assimilation and egestion.
- Case-based items: dental charts, energy in a snack, a blocked bile duct or a malnutrition survey, with a 2-mark part with an internal choice.

questions.stem_md: Each human tooth is fixed in a socket of the jaw bone. This type of attachment is described as
questions.solution_md: Teeth embedded in sockets of the jaw bone are thecodont — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A seven-year-old loses a front tooth, and a few months later a larger tooth grows in its place. Which term describes this feature of human dentition?

options.text_md: Thecodont: teeth are set in sockets of the jaw
Heterodont: teeth are of different types
Diphyodont: a temporary set of milk teeth is replaced by permanent teeth

questions.solution_md: Forming two sets of teeth, deciduous then permanent, is diphyodont dentition — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A dentist’s chart of an adult shows, in each half of each jaw from the front, two incisors, one canine, two premolars and three molars. Which dental formula is this?
questions.solution_md: The order is I, C, PM, M: 2, 1, 2, 3 in each half of the upper and lower jaw, written 2123/2123 — option (b).

questions.stem_md: During swallowing, food does not enter the windpipe because

options.text_md: the epiglottis, a cartilaginous flap, closes the glottis
the gastro-oesophageal sphincter closes the pharynx
the trachea does not open into the pharynx

questions.solution_md: The epiglottis prevents the entry of food into the glottis (opening of the windpipe) during swallowing — option (a).

questions.stem_md: In a slide of the ileum wall, a student sees a layer of loose connective tissue with nerves, blood vessels and lymph vessels, lying between the muscle layers and the innermost lining. This layer is the
questions.solution_md: The sub-mucosa is loose connective tissue containing nerves, blood and lymph vessels, between the muscularis and the mucosa — option (b).

questions.stem_md: What do the microvilli on the cells lining the intestinal villi mainly do?

options.text_md: They secrete hydrochloric acid into the lumen.
They carry chylomicrons to the liver.
They enormously increase the surface area and give a brush border appearance.

questions.solution_md: Microvilli give a brush border appearance and, with villi, increase the surface area enormously — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Bile contains no digestive enzymes. How does it still help in the digestion of fats?

options.text_md: It converts fats directly into glycerol and fatty acids.
It makes the duodenum strongly acidic for lipase.
Its bile salts emulsify fats into very small micelles, and it activates lipases.
It carries fats from the liver to the gall bladder.

questions.solution_md: Bile emulsifies fats, breaking them into very small micelles, and also activates lipases — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A stone lodges in the common hepato-pancreatic duct just above the sphincter of Oddi. Which secretions are prevented from reaching the duodenum?
questions.solution_md: The bile duct and the pancreatic duct open together into the duodenum as the common hepato-pancreatic duct, so a block there stops both — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Which component of saliva acts as an antibacterial agent that helps prevent infections in the mouth?
questions.solution_md: Lysozyme in saliva is antibacterial — option (d).

questions.stem_md: After surgery that removed most of his stomach, a patient develops a deficiency of vitamin B12 even though his diet is unchanged. The best explanation is the loss of

options.text_md: intrinsic factor from the parietal (oxyntic) cells
mucus from the mucus neck cells

questions.solution_md: Parietal or oxyntic cells secrete HCl and intrinsic factor, which is essential for the absorption of vitamin B12 — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A two-month-old baby feeds only on milk. Which enzyme in the baby’s gastric juice especially helps to digest milk proteins?
questions.solution_md: Rennin is a proteolytic enzyme found in the gastric juice of infants which helps in the digestion of milk proteins — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A child is born unable to make enterokinase. Why would the digestion of proteins in the small intestine be badly affected?

options.text_md: Pepsin would not be formed in the stomach.
Bile would not be released by the gall bladder.
Dipeptidases would digest the intestinal wall.
Trypsinogen would not be activated to trypsin, and trypsin is needed to activate the other pancreatic proenzymes.

questions.solution_md: Enterokinase from the intestinal mucosa activates trypsinogen to trypsin, which in turn activates the other enzymes of pancreatic juice — option (d).

questions.stem_md: The products formed when lactase in succus entericus acts on lactose are
questions.solution_md: Lactose is hydrolysed by lactase into glucose and galactose — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Chyme leaving the stomach is very acidic, yet intestinal enzymes work at about pH 7.8. What creates this alkaline medium in the intestine?

options.text_md: Hydrochloric acid from the parietal cells
Bicarbonates from the pancreas with mucus, helped by the sub-mucosal (Brunner’s) glands
Bile pigments from the gall bladder

questions.solution_md: Mucus along with bicarbonates from the pancreas protects the intestinal mucosa from acid and provides an alkaline medium (pH 7.8); Brunner’s glands also help — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Fructose and some amino acids are absorbed with the help of carrier ions such as sodium ions. This mechanism is called
questions.solution_md: Absorption with the help of carrier ions like sodium ions is facilitated transport — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A student traces a drop of dietary fat after it has been digested to fatty acids and glycerol. Which sequence is correct?

options.text_md: Chylomicrons → blood capillaries of villi → micelles → lacteals
Micelles → blood capillaries directly → liver → lacteals
Micelles → intestinal mucosa → chylomicrons → lacteals → blood

questions.solution_md: Insoluble fatty acids and glycerol form micelles, enter the mucosa, are re-formed into protein-coated chylomicrons, enter lacteals and finally reach the blood — option (d).

questions.stem_md: After part of his colon is removed, a patient’s faeces become more watery than before. Which function of the large intestine has been reduced?

options.text_md: Absorption of water and some minerals

questions.solution_md: The large intestine absorbs some water, minerals and certain drugs; no significant digestion occurs there — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Which of these is absorbed in the stomach?

options.text_md: Most amino acids from digested proteins

questions.solution_md: Absorption of water, simple sugars and alcohol occurs in the stomach — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Which statement about defaecation is correct?

options.text_md: It is an involuntary reflex that cannot be controlled.
It is controlled by the vomit centre in the medulla.
It is a voluntary process carried out by a mass peristaltic movement.
It is the absorption of water from faeces in the rectum.

questions.solution_md: Faeces in the rectum start a neural reflex causing the urge; their egestion through the anus is a voluntary process carried out by a mass peristaltic movement — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A man recovering from a liver infection notices that the whites of his eyes and his skin have turned yellow. The yellow colour is due to

options.text_md: deposits of bile pigments, as in jaundice
loss of red blood cells in diarrhoea
excess carotene from the diet in indigestion

questions.solution_md: In jaundice the liver is affected and the skin and eyes turn yellow due to the deposit of bile pigments — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Vomiting, the ejection of stomach contents through the mouth, is a reflex controlled by

options.text_md: the vomit centre in the medulla

questions.solution_md: Vomiting is a reflex action controlled by the vomit centre in the medulla; nausea usually comes first — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A toddler has had frequent, watery stools for three days and has lost weight. Apart from the loss of water, why is she losing weight?

options.text_md: Diarrhoea stops the secretion of saliva.
Diarrhoea makes the liver store more glycogen.
Diarrhoea increases the digestion of fats.
Diarrhoea reduces the absorption of food.

questions.solution_md: Diarrhoea is abnormally frequent bowel movement with more liquid faeces, and it reduces the absorption of food — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A condition in which faeces are retained in the rectum because bowel movements occur irregularly is called
questions.solution_md: Retention of faeces in the rectum from irregular bowel movements is constipation — option (c).

questions.stem_md: After a late-night wedding feast of rich, spicy food, a guest feels uncomfortably full for hours. Which disorder and cause does this best fit?

options.text_md: Jaundice, from deposits of bile pigments
Marasmus, from lack of proteins and calories
Indigestion, from over-eating and spicy food

questions.solution_md: In indigestion food is not properly digested, giving a feeling of fullness; causes include inadequate enzymes, anxiety, food poisoning, over-eating and spicy food — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A two-year-old was weaned early onto a diet of rice water and sugar, which gives enough calories but little protein. He now has swollen legs and belly, thin limbs and poor growth. The condition is
questions.solution_md: Kwashiorkor is protein deficiency with an adequate calorie intake; oedema and swelling, wasting of muscles and thin limbs are typical — option (a).

questions.stem_md: An eight-month-old whose mother’s milk was replaced too early by watery cereal that is poor in both protein and calories becomes extremely thin, with dry, wrinkled skin and no swelling. The condition is
questions.solution_md: Marasmus is a simultaneous deficiency of proteins and calories, usually in infants under a year: extreme emaciation, thin limbs and dry, thin, wrinkled skin — option (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The lining of the stomach is not damaged by the highly concentrated hydrochloric acid of gastric juice.

**Reason (R):** Mucus and bicarbonates in gastric juice lubricate and protect the mucosal epithelium from excoriation by the acid.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both are true, and the protective mucus and bicarbonates explain A — option (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Human beings are diphyodont.

**Reason (R):** The hard chewing surface of human teeth is made of enamel.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both are true, but having two sets of teeth (milk and permanent) is not explained by the enamel of the chewing surface — option (b).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Fatty acids and glycerol are first taken into lacteals rather than directly into the blood.

**Reason (R):** Fatty acids and glycerol are highly soluble in water.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: A is true. R is false: they are insoluble, so they are carried as micelles and then chylomicrons into the lymph vessels (lacteals) — option (c).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Most of the digestion of proteins takes place in the large intestine.

**Reason (R):** No significant digestive activity occurs in the large intestine.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: A is false: proteins are digested in the stomach and small intestine. R is true — option (d).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The small intestine is the principal organ for the absorption of nutrients.

**Reason (R):** Digestion is completed in the small intestine, and its villi and microvilli give it an enormous absorptive surface.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both are true, and R explains why absorption is concentrated in the small intestine — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Distinguish between diarrhoea and constipation.

questions.stem_md: Describe the four layers of the wall of the alimentary canal from the outside inwards.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Serosa:** the outermost layer, a thin **mesothelium** with some connective tissue.

**Muscularis:** smooth muscle, usually an **inner circular** and an **outer longitudinal** layer; an oblique layer in some regions.

**Sub-mucosa:** loose connective tissue with **nerves, blood and lymph vessels**; glands in the duodenum.

**Mucosa:** lines the lumen; forms **rugae** in the stomach and **villi** in the small intestine; has **goblet cells** and forms glands.

questions.stem_md: A student chews a piece of plain bread for three minutes without swallowing and notices that it starts to taste slightly sweet. Explain this, describing both the mechanical and the chemical digestion in the mouth.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Mechanical:** the **teeth and tongue** masticate the bread and mix it with saliva; **mucus** lubricates the particles and helps form a **bolus**.

**Chemical:** saliva contains **salivary amylase**, which at about **pH 6.8** hydrolyses starch into the disaccharide **maltose**; about **30 percent** of starch is digested in the mouth. Maltose tastes sweet. Saliva also has **lysozyme**, an antibacterial agent.

questions.stem_md: State how each of these is absorbed and justify your answer: (i) glucose against its concentration gradient; (ii) fructose; (iii) water.

answer.model_answer_md:
(i) **Active transport**: moving glucose **against a concentration gradient** needs **energy**; amino acids and sodium ions are also absorbed this way.

(ii) **Facilitated transport**: fructose, and some amino acids, are absorbed with the help of **carrier ions such as sodium ions**.

(iii) **Passive transport**: water moves according to the **osmotic gradient**, without energy.

questions.solution_md: Mechanism with reason for each.

questions.stem_md: Trace the path of digested fat from the lumen of the small intestine to the blood, explaining why it does not enter blood capillaries directly.

answer.model_answer_md: Lipases, helped by bile, break fats into **fatty acids and glycerol**. Being **insoluble**, these cannot be absorbed into the blood directly. They are packed into small droplets called **micelles**, which move into the **intestinal mucosa**. There they are re-formed into tiny **protein-coated fat globules, chylomicrons**, which pass into the **lacteals** of the villi. The lymph vessels finally release them into the **blood stream**.

questions.solution_md: Micelles, chylomicrons, lacteals.

questions.stem_md: Name the three main digestive glands and give the location and secretion of each.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Salivary glands:** three pairs — **parotids** (cheek), **sub-maxillary or sub-mandibular** (lower jaw) and **sub-linguals** (below the tongue) — secrete **saliva**.

**Liver:** the largest gland, about **1.2–1.5 kg**, below the diaphragm; its hepatic cells secrete **bile**, stored in the gall bladder.

**Pancreas:** between the limbs of the C-shaped duodenum; secretes alkaline **pancreatic juice** (and the hormones insulin and glucagon).

questions.stem_md: After drinking contaminated water at a fair, a boy has repeated vomiting and watery stools. Explain each of these disorders, and why he soon feels weak and dehydrated.

answer.model_answer_md: **Vomiting** is the ejection of stomach contents through the mouth, a **reflex** controlled by the **vomit centre in the medulla**, usually preceded by **nausea**. **Diarrhoea** is an abnormal frequency of bowel movement with **more liquid faeces**; such inflammation of the intestinal tract is often due to **bacterial or viral infection**. Both cause **loss of water and salts**, and diarrhoea **reduces the absorption of food**, so he becomes dehydrated and weak.

questions.solution_md: Vomiting, diarrhoea, consequences.

questions.stem_md: Describe the human alimentary canal from the mouth to the anus, naming the regions of the stomach and of the small and large intestines, and describe the general structure of its wall.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Mouth and pharynx.** The mouth leads to the **buccal cavity**, with **32 thecodont, diphyodont and heterodont teeth** (dental formula 2123/2123) and a muscular **tongue**, attached to the floor by the **frenulum** and bearing papillae, some with taste buds. The short **pharynx** is a common passage for food and air; the **epiglottis** guards the glottis.

**Oesophagus and stomach.** The thin, long **oesophagus** passes through the neck, thorax and diaphragm to the **J-shaped stomach**, guarded by the gastro-oesophageal sphincter. The stomach, in the upper left abdomen, has a **cardiac** portion, a **fundic** region and a **pyloric** portion.

**Small intestine.** The pyloric sphincter opens into the **C-shaped duodenum**, followed by the long coiled **jejunum** and the highly coiled **ileum**.

**Large intestine.** The ileum opens into the **caecum**, a blind sac with symbiotic micro-organisms, from which the **vermiform appendix** arises; then the **colon** (ascending, transverse, descending and sigmoid) and the **rectum**, which opens at the **anus**.

**Wall.** From oesophagus to rectum there are four layers: **serosa** (mesothelium), **muscularis** (inner circular and outer longitudinal smooth muscle), **sub-mucosa** (loose connective tissue with nerves, blood and lymph vessels) and **mucosa**, which forms rugae in the stomach and villi with microvilli in the small intestine.

questions.solution_md: Regions and wall.

questions.stem_md: Describe the salivary glands, liver and pancreas: their position, structure where relevant, secretions, and how the secretions of the liver and pancreas reach the duodenum.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Salivary glands.** Three pairs produce most of the saliva: the **parotids** in the cheeks, the **sub-maxillary (sub-mandibular)** glands in the lower jaw and the **sub-linguals** below the tongue. Saliva contains electrolytes, **salivary amylase**, **lysozyme** and mucus.

**Liver.** The largest gland, about **1.2 to 1.5 kg** in an adult, lies just below the diaphragm and has **two lobes**. Its structural and functional units are **hepatic lobules**, with hepatic cells in cords, each lobule covered by **Glisson’s capsule**. Hepatic cells secrete **bile**, which passes through the **hepatic ducts** and is stored and concentrated in the **gall bladder**. The **cystic duct** joins the hepatic duct to form the **common bile duct**.

**Pancreas.** A compound, elongated organ between the limbs of the C-shaped duodenum. Its **exocrine** part secretes alkaline **pancreatic juice** containing enzymes; its **endocrine** part secretes **insulin and glucagon**.

**Route to the duodenum.** The bile duct and the **pancreatic duct** open together into the duodenum as the **common hepato-pancreatic duct**, guarded by the **sphincter of Oddi**.

questions.solution_md: Three glands and the duct system.

questions.stem_md: Describe the digestion of carbohydrates, proteins and fats as food passes through the alimentary canal, naming the enzymes, where they act and the products formed.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Carbohydrates.** In the **mouth**, salivary amylase (pH 6.8) hydrolyses about 30 percent of starch into **maltose**. In the **small intestine**, **pancreatic amylase** converts the remaining polysaccharides into **disaccharides**. Enzymes of **succus entericus** finish the job: **maltase** gives glucose, **lactase** gives glucose and galactose, and **sucrase** gives glucose and fructose.

**Proteins.** In the **stomach**, HCl converts pepsinogen into **pepsin**, which at pH 1.8 changes proteins into **proteoses and peptones**; in infants **rennin** digests milk proteins. In the **duodenum**, enterokinase activates **trypsinogen** to trypsin, which activates the other proenzymes; **trypsin, chymotrypsin and carboxypeptidase** form **dipeptides**, and **dipeptidases** of succus entericus give **amino acids**.

**Fats.** Gastric glands secrete small amounts of lipase. In the small intestine **bile** emulsifies fats into micelles and activates **lipases**, which give di- and **monoglycerides**; intestinal lipases complete the breakdown into **fatty acids and glycerol**.

Breakdown of these biomacromolecules occurs mainly in the **duodenum**, and the simple products are absorbed in the jejunum and ileum; the intestinal medium is kept alkaline (pH 7.8).

questions.solution_md: Enzymes, sites, products.

questions.stem_md: What is absorption? Explain the mechanisms of absorption of digested food, the absorption of fats, and the absorption that takes place in different parts of the alimentary canal. End by explaining assimilation and egestion.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Absorption** is the process by which the end products of digestion pass through the intestinal mucosa into the **blood or lymph**.

**Mechanisms.** Small amounts of glucose, amino acids and chloride ions are absorbed by **simple diffusion**, down a concentration gradient. Fructose and some amino acids are absorbed with **carrier ions such as sodium ions** (**facilitated transport**). Water follows the **osmotic gradient**. **Active transport** moves amino acids, glucose and sodium ions **against the concentration gradient**, using energy.

**Fats.** Insoluble fatty acids and glycerol form **micelles**, enter the mucosa, are re-formed into **chylomicrons** and pass into the **lacteals**, which later empty into the blood.

**Different parts.** In the **mouth**, certain drugs are absorbed through the mucosa below the tongue. The **stomach** absorbs water, simple sugars and alcohol. The **small intestine** is the principal organ of absorption: glucose, fructose, fatty acids, glycerol and amino acids. The **large intestine** absorbs water, some minerals and drugs.

**Assimilation** is the use of absorbed substances by the tissues for their activities. **Egestion**: faeces in the rectum start a neural reflex, and **defaecation** through the anus is a **voluntary** process carried out by a mass peristaltic movement.

questions.solution_md: Definition, mechanisms, fats, sites, assimilation, egestion.

questions.stem_md: A health blogger writes: “The stomach digests everything we eat, and the small intestine is just a tube that carries food to the colon, so losing part of it would not affect nutrition.” Evaluate this claim, using what you know about digestion and absorption.

answer.model_answer_md:
**“The stomach digests everything.”** Incorrect. The stomach only begins protein digestion: pepsin converts proteins into proteoses and peptones, rennin acts on milk proteins in infants, and only small amounts of lipase are secreted. Carbohydrate digestion starts in the mouth, and most of it, and nearly all fat digestion, happen in the small intestine.

**“The small intestine is just a tube.”** Incorrect. In the duodenum, bile emulsifies fats; pancreatic juice supplies trypsin, chymotrypsin, carboxypeptidase, amylase, lipases and nucleases; and succus entericus supplies maltase, lactase, sucrase, dipeptidases and nucleosidases. Breakdown of biomacromolecules occurs mainly in the duodenum.

**Absorption.** The jejunum and ileum are the principal sites of absorption. Villi and microvilli give an enormous surface, with capillaries for glucose and amino acids and lacteals for fats carried as chylomicrons. Absorption uses diffusion, facilitated transport and active transport. The large intestine absorbs only water, some minerals and drugs, with no significant digestion.

**Judgement.** The claim is wrong. Losing a large part of the small intestine would reduce both digestion and absorption, leading to poor nutrition and weight loss, as happens when absorption is reduced in diarrhoea.

questions.solution_md: Each part evaluated; judgement.
